speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the action taken in both the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States to boost the tariff on copper, can the minister tell the house if proper representations are being made by the Canadian government in order to prevent the imposition of higher tariffs against Canadian copper?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might attempt to answer the question asked by the hon. member, because a similar question was asked of me yesterday by another hon. member, arising out of press reports from Washington to the effect that bills had been introduced in the United States congress seeking the application of tariffs against imports of Canadian copper.
I have made inquiries. I find that bills have been introduced in the House of Representatives and in the United States Senate by individual members of those bodies. There is no indication, and the government has no reason to suppose, that these bills have been introduced with any approval on the part of the United States administration. Copies of the bills have not yet been received, but it is expected that copies may be available to this government shortly.
The United States tariff is bound at 1.8 cents per pound. At the present time copper enters the United States duty free under United States legislation which expires on June 30 next. In that legislation there is a provision that if the price falls below 24 cents per pound the normal tax of 1.8 cents per pound will be restored. However, press reports indicate that the bills which have been introduced of course go much further.

maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext: I have a supplementary question. Does the minister not think it might be prudent to get in touch with the government of the United States in order to make sure that no boost in tariffs is made?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext: If there is any reason at all to think these bills will be likely to be advanced in congress, there is no doubt about the type of action the Canadian government will take. Certainly steps will be taken to repeat the views of the Canadian government with regard to this and associated subjects whenever there is any reason at all to do so. I may add that, so far as the legislative position is concerned, much depends upon what action the United States congress itself takes with regard to the trade agreements legislation which will expire on June 30 unless renewed by congress. That matter, in a word, is at the base of many of these problems.

maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of Finance, in answer to my question respecting the proposed tariff on lead and zinc, said there was no formal protest in writing made to the United States authorities. I want to ask the minister if he would consider making a formal protest in writing to the President of the United States respecting this proposed increase in tariff.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext:
I intended, Mr. Speaker, as soon as there was an opportunity this morning to rise and say that the answer I gave the hon. member yesterday was made without referring to the file, and needs to be amended. I find on checking the file that on July 19,	1957, a message was sent to
Washington, with a formal note attached to it from the Canadian government; and that formal note was presented to the department of state of the United States respecting proposals of the United States administration indicating an increase in the tariff on lead and zinc. I am informed that the note was delivered on July 23, and a formal reply was received from the department of state on August 2.
I take it I may anticipate from my hon. friend a request for the tabling of that note and the reply, and I think I may assure him now that a request will be made in the ordinary way to the United States government looking to the release of both notes for tabling in the house.

maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext:
I am not so interested in the tabling of the note. What I am interested in is, will the minister make the protest directly to the President of the United States, who is responsible in this matter?

Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know that it lies within my power to make a protest directly to the President of the United States. There are established channels for the presentation of communications between governments, but the hon. member may be very sure that the views of the Canadian government have been fully presented to the United States government and will continue to be impressed upon them.
So far as personal communications are concerned, I may say that when Mr. Dulles visited Ottawa last summer this matter was discussed with him, first by the Prime Minister and then by the Prime Minister and two other members of this government. The matter was fully discussed at Washington in early October at the time of the meeting of the continuing committee on Canada-United States trade and economic matters, and the subject has been referred to in subsequent discussions. It was referred to in my talks with Mr. Anderson, the secretary of the treasury, in Paris in December. My hon. friend may be well assured that the views of the Canadian government have been put before the United States authorities repeatedly. They fully understand what deep concern we entertain at the prospect of the imposition of tariffs by the United States against importations of Canadian lead and zinc.
My hon. friend is aware, I am sure, that under the existing agreements under GATT the imposition of such tariffs would constitute a breach of the provisions unless there were renegotiations. I presume that if the United States administration feel that they must proceed with the course that has been suggested, they will be asking for renegotiation with respect to these items. The view of the Canadian government will be firmly held, my friend may be assured.

maintopic: LEAD, ZINC AND COPPER    INQUIRY AS TO STEPS TO PROTECT CANADIAN INTERESTS
speechtext:
May
I ask a supplementary question. Can the Minister of Finance inform the house whether he thinks the efforts of the Canadian government in this matter will finally meet with success?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: EFFECT ON CANADA OF PROPOSED EUROPEAN FREE TRADE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of continued reports of progress in the setting up of the European free trade zone. Would


the minister inform the house what representations have been made to these countries? In what way does the government feel this will affect Canadian trade, particularly with regard to agricultural products? Can the minister say whether any active consideration is being given by the Canadian government to associating Canada in any way with such a free trade zone?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: EFFECT ON CANADA OF PROPOSED EUROPEAN FREE TRADE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject has been under discussion in the house before. We are watching developments in Europe very closely. We are not making any immediate representations. At the conference of NATO held in Geneva toward the end of October we dealt with the subject of the common market that was to be developed in Europe. I made a statement on behalf of the government of Canada concerning our attitude in that regard and our concern with respect to the sale of our agricultural products in Europe. I was assured in the speeches made by the members of the participating nations that due regard would be had to the points that were made in that speech.
At the moment we have no information that Canada's trade will be adversely affected by events transpiring in Europe. In fact, I think in the long run there will be increased trade between Canada and the six nations of Europe.

maintopic: EFFECT ON CANADA OF PROPOSED EUROPEAN FREE TRADE ZONE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might ask a supplementary question. My question had rather more to do with the 17-nation free trading area. Have we decided to stay out of it entirely?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that free trade area comprising 17 nations has not advanced to the stage at which any action is necessary on the part of ourselves or anyone else. Certainly we are watching it very closely. Once again, we feel that in so far as we can judge by what we have heard from other nations interested in that area, Canadian interests will not be adversely affected.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Public Works. Was the minister enunciating government housing policy when he said in Toronto on Thursday night to delegates to the fifteenth annual convention of the housebuilders' association that builders could expect little or no help from the government in the future? More specifically, does this mean that the government will refuse to grant further money for direct lending through N.H.A. if the supply of mortgage money from conventional lenders continues to decline?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON FEDERAL AID BY MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS
speechtext: In reply to this question I would suggest to the hon. member that it is extremely unwise to believe everything he reads in the papers. The statement he has just read is completely inaccurate in its attempt to report what I said at this convention. I did say, as I said in the house in discussing the bill amending the National Housing Act, that neither this government nor any other government could provide all the money which would be required for home building in Canada. We are hoping that in the year 1958 there will be 140,000 starts. If that objective is reached it will be the largest number of homes that have ever been started in Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at ten o'clock last night I was making a few comments on observations which had been made by hon. members opposite in regard to Bill No. 237. In the main they contained a series of contradictions and pious hopes.
The hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough made a quite amazing statement when he said he was in complete support of this measure because it was going to be an incentive to the farmers of his riding for greater production. That seems rather strange when we are aware that Hansard records over and over again the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that one of the principles embodied in this measure is that it will not be an incentive for increased production.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member is attempting to put in my mouth words on this subject which I did not say. I said this legislation was of a type which would make it possible to prevent the accumulation of large surpluses, which is quite a different matter than the one he has just mentioned.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.

The minister is playing with words; and the very fact that he has said over and over again that he has the prerogative of introducing a guaranteed price, either above or below the base price, is a clear indication of what the minister and the government have in mind. So the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough has been led down the garden path in this regard, and the most amazing thing is that he is quite prepared to go back to his constituency and lead the parade of his farmers down that path.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
The only other comment I was going to make with regard to what was said by hon. members yesterday was with respect to the comments of the hon. member for Saskatoon. He said he was very happy and proud that the revolving fund now contains $250 million with which the minister could implement this very far-reaching and progressive piece of legislation. The only hitch in that is that the revolving fund does not revolve, and from past experience we know it is not going to revolve.
He then placed considerable emphasis on the advisory committee. He said this is a wonderful committee and it is going to do great things. I would suggest to him that we on this side of the house are not so naive as to fall for that line; because after all, who are these people who are going to be appointed by the minister to constitute this advisory committee of which the hon. member for Saskatoon is so proud? They are the


very people who have been around this house ever since the bill was introduced trying to convince the minister that he should take their advice. Now the minister is saying, "When I set up the committee I am going to put representatives of farm organizations on it and I am going to take their advice as to what to do." These are the same people who have been trying to advise the minister on what he should do now. He has not taken their advice; and I do not think anybody, or any farmer, is going to be impressed very much with that kind of argument.
To use the words of the Minister of Agriculture this bill is a step and a start toward the implementation of a comprehensive agricultural policy. The minister said this was a start. Well, we are on the second start now, and possibly before we finish we will be starting for the third time. If the third start, which I hope we will make, is not any better than the first two starts, I suggest that if the minister has any idea that this is the introduction of a comprehensive agricultural policy he has picked about the worst possible place from which to start.
Our attitude to this revised edition of Bill No. 237 is exactly the same as it was toward the original bill. I am the first to admit that five new amendments have been introduced, but I still maintain that when you multiply zero by five the result is still zero. That is about the best I can say for this new, revised edition.
One amazing thing is that when the minister introduced his revised version of this bill he made it clear over and over again that the bill was not changed in the least, but after he had spoken for a few minutes he came up with the proposition that the government should be commended because they had made changes in the bill at the request of farm organizations and in line with the thinking of those organizations. As a result, we are not sure whether the minister believes the bill is the same or whether he has in fact made changes.
Some of these changes appear, on the surface, as if there is something worth while in them; but having said that the changes have been made in line with the thinking of the farm organizations and that the changes are worth while, the minister attempts to cover up the shortcomings of the bill by spending a good deal of his time comparing it with the old act.
I must say to him that I am still of the opinion that this bill is not as good as the one which is presently on the statute books of this country, because the whole secret of this bill, the whole key to its success, lies in the pricing formula which the government

has seen fit to use. Clause 8 is the key to the whole position, and because there is no parity formula the bill is doomed to failure. There is no guarantee. One thing to which I take great exception is the fact that there is some dishonesty in the way in which this bill is drawn up in regard to clause 8.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. May I remind the hon. member that the word "dishonesty" is not one which is considered parliamentary if it is brought to bear on any of the hon. members of the house, and it seems to me he is coming close to doing that.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite prepared to withdraw. I did not mean it to apply in any disparaging way to the minister, but I say there is an inference in the legislation which is not correct. The minister has told us he is going to establish a base price and that afterwards he is going to take it upon himself to set guaranteed prices either above or below the base price. I am not convinced that the committee he intends to set up will have very much if anything to say about the guaranteed price. So the situation may arise where the consumers of this country will be led to believe that the farmer is getting 110 per cent or 120 per cent of the base price, in consequence of which they will certainly be much concerned. They are going to believe that the farmer is getting 120 per cent of a just price, when actually that price will be below a parity price.
The minister suggested that the Agricultural Prices Support Act was inadequate, and that any price which was set was an ad hoc price, as he put it. I suggest that the bill before us now still administers guaranteed prices in exactly the same way. Any prices fixed under it will be ad hoc prices, for the reason that the present formula is not tied to a parity price or to any formula, so they will have to be fixed of necessity on the basis of a decision by the minister, and that kind of decision is nothing but an ad hoc decision.
The 80 per cent floor with regard to the products the bill does affect is calculated over a 10-year moving average of market prices. The minister did not tell the house that this 80 per cent floor, based on present day prices, is still less than 70 per cent of parity prices. He was very anxious to make it clear that in the 10-year moving average we would get the advantage of four of the best years agriculture has seen in this country for some time. But we are going to lose those four years because of the fact that this is a moving average; we are going to take up a new year and drop one of the old years until, in four years time, we will lose entirely the advantage of those four good years of which the minister is so proud.
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, as well as other organizations, has done a very comprehensive survey of what is implied in this legislation so far as the 10-year moving average is concerned. It has come up with a series of figures dealing with the nine products covered by the bill to show what is going to happen. Take hogs, for instance. The average price in 1957 for grade B1 hogs was $30.37 at Toronto. The C.F.A., who have been suggesting over the years that the government should adopt its agricultural policy which favours 70 per cent of parity- a policy which has been frowned on over the years by other agricultural organizations- points out that its 70 per cent of parity formula is far ahead of the government's proposed measure; that its price of 70 per cent of parity amounts to $23.51 as against the government's suggested 1958 price of $23.36. Then the organization goes on to say that should the average price in the next 4 years apply as in the last four years, that is $27.93, the minimum guaranteed 10-year average market price for 1962 would be $22.40 compared with the 1958 estimated price of $23.36.
The same is true in the case of butter. The average price in 1957 was 60.6 cents. The C.F.A. proposal is for a price of 50.1 cents. Eighty per cent of the ten-year moving average as presently suggested by the government is 49.6 cents. The C.F.A. goes on to say that if the price of butter in the next four years remains as it has in the last four years, by 1962 the price for butter under this proposition will have dropped to 48.4 cents.
I am not going to go through the whole list of commodities, but there is a similar drop for each. Good steers at Toronto in 1957 averaged $18.95 on the market. Under the C.F.A. proposal $17.62 would be the minimum price, but the minimum price for 1958 under this legislation will be $17.44. The C.F.A. points out that if the price of steers on the market over the next four years remains at about the same level as it has in the last four years then by 1962, according to this moving ten-year scale, the price will have dropped to $15.89.
I am sure the minister will say, "Well, we will introduce our guaranteed price if we think the price does not represent production costs," but of course that price is not calculated in the market price, which is the price on which the ten-year average is computed.
We witnessed an interesting spectacle the other day. Eggs were selling on the market in western Canada for something in the neighbourhood of 28 cents a dozen to producers. I am receiving letters every day
3466	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization from people complaining that they are forced to accept 28.5 cents a dozen for eggs. When the minister was questioned about this he said, "Yes, we are guaranteeing the packer 38 cents and have asked him to pay 30 cents to the producer." However, the packer said it was impossible to operate with an 8 cent margin and make a profit. The minister rose in this house and said, "I have attempted to make an arrangement with the packer." In effect he said to the packer, "You pay the farmer 30 cents, and you and I will work out some arrangement to compensate you for the loss you suggest you have to take over the 8 cents."
Under this measure I suggest there is nothing to stop the processors from driving the price on the market down to the 80 per cent floor, and that is where it is going to go. The minister has told members of this house and the farmers of Canada over and over again that he realizes there is no parity principle involved in the pricing formula he is going to employ, but he says, "You will just have to trust me and the Conservative government. I am going to see to it that the farmer is going to get his cost of production. He is going to get something in the neighbourhood of parity prices, if you will just trust me."
He then spent a considerable amount of time criticizing the only system on this continent that ever attempted to give the farmer a parity price, the United States farm program. How does the minister think the farmer can place any trust in a minister of the government who says, "I am going to give you a parity price," and then spends most of his allotted time running down and discrediting the only government on this continent that ever made a real effort to give the farmer a parity price?
What about this board that is going to be set up to advise the minister in regard to production costs and those commodities that should be supported? On reading the measure very carefully is it the duty of the board to make sure that the prescribed price or the guaranteed price bears a fair relationship-to parity? No; to the base price. That is the function of this board. What products is it going to recommend to the minister for support? Only those products the minister tells the board he thinks should oe supported. In effect the duty of this board is to do what the minister tells it to do, nothing more and nothing less.
I wonder why the minister did not see fit to include western grain in this support measure. Does he think the western wheat, barley and oats producer is now getting a price that bears a fair relationship to his 

cost of production and therefore does not warrant having those products supported? Surely the minister knows as well as I do that the farmer's cost of production has risen by 50 per cent and continues to rise, while the prices for these grain products have fallen by over 21 per cent during the last few years.
When I was home during the Christmas recess I visited the Massey Harris dealer at Tisdale, where I live. He told me that a new model 92 self-propelled combine will sell next year, if anyone is gullible enough to buy one, for $8,000. This is a machine that sold for $3,450 in 1946 when my brothers and I bought one at that price. The minister is going to have to take a close look at the proposition of supporting grain prices in western Canada.
What about soy beans and sugar beets? What is going to happen to the sugar beet grower whose product is already being supported under the Agricultural Prices Support Act? As soon as this measure becomes the law of the land he will be left out in the cold, because the Agricultural Prices Support Act will not operate after the adoption of the measure that is before us.
"A forward price," said the minister, "on the basis of one year." What kind of a forward price is a one-year forward price for the man who is engaged in livestock production? None at all. It is not worth the paper it is written on. I would suggest that the minister should either expand that forward price principle or take it out of the bill altogether, because it is absolutely useless, just as useless as the committee he is going to set up. I would also suggest that clause 5 of the bill relating to this committee should be deleted entirely, unless the minister is prepared to give this committee more power than he proposes to give it at the present time.
If this bill is going to mean anything I suggest that it must have as its fundamental the principle of parity prices. That is the only thing that is going to give the farmer any security on the land. It is not a question of giving the farmer a profit on his operation; that is not envisaged in a parity price. It simply means that there shall be a fair relationship between his cost of production and the price he receives for the commodity he produces.
If the minister is so anxious to have an advisory board composed of representatives of agricultural producers, then I urge that he accept the proposal this group is putting forward and have the agriculture committee of this house meet and invite the farm organizations to come down here and advise the minister as to the kind of legislation which

they would like to have a hand in administering. That is the only fair, reasonable and logical approach to this whole question.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak in support of this agricultural bill, No. 237. The amendments recommended by the minister after much deliberation have most certainly improved the bill, which is now sound and comprehensive.
I feel sure our agriculture committee have rendered real service through the part they took in the revision of this bill. The minister is to be commended for his attitude of tolerance and fair consideration to the many suggestions offered by members of our committee. Agriculture was at the crossroads. This fact was recognized by members of our party before we came to power. Because the powers that be in our ranks were aware of this problem, they promised to do something about it. The agricultural industry has placed its confidence in us, and certainly we do not intend to let it down.
Early action was taken to save the turkey and fowl industry. This was a preview of what was to come from an alert and active government. At this time I am going to quote an excerpt from a letter I received last November:
Just in case you haven't been given the latest figures on turkeys, we in Canada are enjoying decent turkey prices since John Diefenbaker took his action on barring American birds. The farm prices here for live turkeys at the farm are about 35 cents to 38 cents per pound whereas in the United States they are only 18 cents to 20 cents at the farm. Chicken broilers are now 20 cents to 201 cents as compared with 16 cents in the U.S.A. So few of the Canadian farmers know of these advantages, which is really a tragedy.
This bill will introduce the first complete relief of distressed conditions the farmers have had in many years. It means that a way of life will be sustained for thousands of people who have been reluctant to leave their farms. Many others will now be able to make a livelihood without going into the towns and cities and taking supplementary work. This latter group are mostly young farmers who, in having to secure such work to bolster their incomes, displaced a group of older workers. The former government ignored the plight of those older citizens who were unable to find employment yet were not old enough to benefit from pensions.
This agricultural bill will certainly relieve this situation, Mr. Speaker. Agriculture accounts for the largest share of the earning power in my constituency. Therefore the assurance of a fair share of the national income will make this bill popular with my people. They may now intelligently plan for the future.
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
My riding of Grey North, located on the southern shores of Georgian bay, is ideal for the production of choice apples. Over 3,000 acres are now in production of the select and most popular varieties. The growers have been continually in difficulty in marketing their crops in competition with United States growers on our markets. This bill does not specifically mention apples, Mr. Speaker, but they can be taken care of as a designated commodity under clause 2. I would suggest at this time that if the grade of United States apples coming into Ontario could be raised so that only the better grades could be imported, much of the difficulty now experienced in the marketing of our apples would disappear.
In essence this bill is an example of true democracy, in view of the fact that the minister will select from the ranks of the farmers an advisory board with which he will meet in consultation at least twice a year. Decisions and plans that these men and our Minister of Agriculture may make from time to time regarding this legislation will certainly bring security and stability to the industry. This bill should be supported on general principles.
When the farmers have money our general economy is good. Never in the history of our country were so many of our farm buildings so badly in need of repair and paint. Many of our farmers are struggling with obsolete machinery which should be replaced. Fencing and other improvement programs were almost completely neglected. Financial obligations have been deferred, spreading symptoms of recession to many other lines of business.
On my visits to the agricultural fairs or fall shows in my riding I found many of the officials very discouraged, even to the point of suggesting that the shows be discontinued. I feel that if the shows should cease to carry on a tremendous loss to the farmer's way of life would result. It would be depressing to the young people who have planned since their childhood to stay with the farms. Their calf clubs would suffer, along with the many other branches of agriculture in which the young people annually compete. This is a direct result of the neglect of the agricultural industry by the former administration. Furthermore, it is common knowledge that in no other industry do people work such long hours for so small a reward. This agricultural bill, Mr. Speaker, will restore confidence and buying power in our rural population, and it could be the spark that would rejuvenate this tired and weary industry.
In conclusion I believe, as Abraham Lincoln once said, "The government must not do for

This bill is the one which the minister has stated is going to do so much for agriculture. During the last election campaign it was stated that if the Conservative party were elected they would institute a system of parity prices, and would guarantee agriculture its fair share of the national income. When we examine the bill we find that there is not any place in the bill any formula whatever which will guarantee parity prices, nor is there any formula which will guarantee that agriculture receives its fair share of the national income.
During the election campaign they also said they would increase our markets for agricultural products. As a matter of fact the only thing the present government has done is to make a threat to the United States that they were going to reduce imports from that country by some 15 per cent. This government has not done much to increase agricultural markets. It is results which count. Certainly the government has sent costly missions over to Britain, but no practical results have been forthcoming as yet. It is time we received some results from the activities of those different missions, if they are ever going to amount to anything. That indication has not been forthcoming thus far.


The government introduced the resolution preceding this bill on December 11. It was on that occasion that the Minister of Agriculture himself stated in this house that this bill embodied the policy of the Conservative party. In fact he went so far as to say this, as recorded in Hansard at page 2189 of December 11, 1957:
I think this legislation will do everything we promised we would do so far as our campaign pledges are concerned.
I therefore think I can say that the first bill which was introduced embodied wholly and completely the Conservative policy after the Minister of Agriculture, as he said in this house, had consulted all the backbenchers with regard to the matter; and we never heard any protest from the Conservative members. We have not yet heard any protest in this house by Conservative members against this bill. There have been a great many protests from the Social Credit party, the C.C.F. party and farm organizations all across this country. Certainly they are not satisfied with the results that have been brought forth in this bill. There is still no formula for parity prices. There is still no formula to institute a cost-price relationship. There is nothing whatever to show that farmers are going to get their fair share of the national income.
I now want to refer in general to the bill. I know that at this time I cannot refer to specific sections and deal with those sections minutely or in detail. However, I want to make reference to the general principle of the bill. I want to say at once that there are one or two good points in it, I think.

What I was going to say was this, and I am speaking about the principle. There is now a preamble to the bill-and as far as I recall that is one of the two places where there is improvement-where a cost-price relationship is referred to. That was one of the things the Conservatives promised they were going to institute as their policy. It should be remembered that in discussing any legislation which is brought before this house, nothing in a preamble has anything whatever to do with the bill itself. I therefore think we can disregard that reference entirely, because certainly the present government never intended to have anything which is said in the preamble apply to the bill itself or they would have put it in the bill.
There are three things in general which the government is introducing under this agricultural legislation. The first is the base price, the second is the floor price and the third is the prescribed or forward price. If I may, I should like to deal first with the base price. The base price was brought to us first as a three-year moving average, namely the last three years. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that this was Conservative policy after complete consideration and in consultation with all the Conservative backbenchers. Hence they all agreed with this three-year policy. No objection was raised in the house, and they said they were proud of the bill.
The three-year moving average was calculated at a time when agricultural prices were beginning to go lower. When the opposition members of this house pointed out how inadequate that would be, and how unsatisfactory it was to the agriculturists of this nation, because of that opposition the government was forced to change this period from three years to ten years.
A while ago I said there were possibly two places that showed some improvement, and this is the second one. When that change from the three-year to the ten-year moving average was made I think the base price would have been slightly better because, of course, in the first years of that ten-year period the prices were fairly good. But as that moving period advances the base price goes down, because there is every indication that the agricultural income is going to continue to fall. If that happens, of course the base price continues to get lower and lower.
We Social Crediters have contended that this period should be fixed so there would be some fair relationship to the cost when we are establishing this base period. The
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization Minister of Agriculture says that would be a terrible thing, that it was never government policy. When we read back we will find out whether or not it was government policy; and I wish to refer to remarks made in the house yesterday by the hon. member for Fraser Valley when he referred to the Prime Minister's definition of parity. I think this is worth putting on the record, especially when one remembers that this was a statement made during the election campaign.
Of course I do not want to start a fight between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture, but the Prime Minister knew very clearly what a set period was. He knew the advantages to agriculture of having such a period, although the Minister of Agriculture does not think that is so-after the election. Let me read what the Prime Minister said when defining parity:
. Parity prices are the dollars and cents prices that give to farm products the same buying or purchasing power they had in a selected base period.
Can you understand that? That is a selected base period, not a moving period.

Mr. Speaker, when we rose at one o'clock I was endeavouring to give the government some good advice, pointing out that I thought the bill was falling far short of what the farmers and the country were expecting.
I wish to make another reference to this bill and in particular to clause 7. Clause 7


is the one part of the bill which does make reference to the cost of production and it states:
The board shall from time to time in accordance with this act take such action as is necessary to stabilize the prices of agricultural commodities at their respective prescribed prices, and shall take such action and make such recommendations as are necessary to ensure that the prescribed prices for an agricultural commodity in effect from time to time shall bear a fair relationship to the base price for such commodity.
As that clause stands it is nonsensical, and I am sure the government will bring in an amendment to it. If they do not bring in an amendment, they should. The last sentence: "shall bear a fair relationship to the base price for such commodity" clearly needs amendment. The word "base" is certainly not the one intended, and I suggest to the government that it should be changed to the word "cost". But although this section does refer to cost-price relationship it is only under that part which deals with the duties of the board, and this could in no way affect the price of the products unless the minister himself so decides. Once again this is left to the discretion of the minister. He can do anything he likes, and I do not think that is a good thing.
When I was speaking on the resolution I pointed out that I thought one of the main purposes the government had in mind in bringing in this legislation was to curtail production. In the course of this debate the minister has pointed out that something must be done to handle farm surpluses, and when I made the remarks I did during the resolution stage he said I was completely wrong and that I was misrepresenting him. On that occasion, as I intend to do now, I referred to his remarks on page 2186 of Hansard on the subject. This is what he said:
I have endeavoured in this legislation to provide for the greatest possible degree of flexibility so we will not be saddled-
I want hon. members to note that word "saddled."
-with a program which inevitably acts as an incentive to produce burdensome and unsaleable surpluses.
If that does not mean that the minister has in mind some method of getting rid of these "burdensome and unsaleable surpluses" I should like to know what it does mean. That this was uppermost in the minister's mind is indicated by the fact that on two other occasions in the course of his speech he made reference to the same subject. I am not going to quote these references now because I did so on the resolution stage. The minister went to some lengths to point out that I was entirely wrong.

I wish to quote an article from the Calgary Herald. The Calgary Herald must be considered to be a very worthwhile newspaper, because there is no paper in Canada which is more Conservative. Certainly it would not misrepresent the minister, and if it has done so the minister should get up and say that he has been misrepresented. This is the article which appeared on Thursday, December 31 on the editorial page. It is entitled: "No Cure-all but Good Medicine." Good medicine for the farmers, I guess. The article reads:
The dominion government in general and agriculture minister D. H. Harkness in particular are both to be commended for the political courage displayed in introduction of the Farm Price Stabilization Bill, more details of which were made known here the other day by Mr. Harkness.

The proposed support prices are so designed that, should a surplus begin to build up, the government will attempt to cut production in the surplus area and, more specifically, will reduce the support price to remove the incentive for growing or producing the particular product of which a surplus is building up.
The next paragraph is a gem, and it states government policy, make no mistake about it.

Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit party has advocated a two-price system for agriculture, a system which would give in the domestic field a parity price for agricultural products. I will not define parity again because I gave the Prime Minister's definition of that a little while ago. On the export markets we would have to take what is generally known as the world price. That should be supplemented by a price support, a deficiency payment or what we Social Crediters have often described as a price discount. All three terms mean about the same thing. We have advocated this system for years. When you consider the income from the domestic and export markets under such a system agriculturists would then be receiving their fair share of the national income. There is nothing like that in this bill. As a matter of fact, as the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) said last evening, there is nothing in this bill which is very different from what was contained in the Agricultural Prices Support Act. subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I am not rising merely with the object of repeating arguments that have already been advanced for or against this bill. I believe this bill contains the germ of a measure that may in the future result in benefits to a great number of farmers. I also am not rising with the purpose of just adding another speech to my record. I understand that that is the strategy of some of the political parties in this house. Hon. members in those splinter groups rise on every possible occasion and speak on. every conceivable subject merely in order to accumulate a formidable list of speeches which they can present to their
3474	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization constituents at election time in the fond hope that their constituents will believe that volume and verbosity can take the place of common sense. I hope that not too many hon. members of this house will follow that practice. Neither is it my intention in speaking at this time to concentrate my criticism on the government which is the practice of the splinter groups because I think the members of the government before June 10 were in the same position as the splinter groups were in that they did not think they would have any more responsibility than the splinter groups would have after the June 10 election.
No one who has been associated with governments for any length of time can fail to realize the difficulties that governments have in attempting to formulate agricultural and other policies that will be acceptable to the people of Canada from Newfoundland to British Columbia before legislation can be enacted and become the law of the land. I think all of us will agree that in the past years much progress has been made by the former federal government in formulating policies under those difficult circumstances.
In spite of the criticism of the splinter groups I can assure you that many Canadians have fared very well under the policies formulated by the Liberal government and perhaps they will continue to fare in this fashion if they apply themselves to the task under Conservative policies as long as they last. However, if the Conservative policies last too long they certainly will not work to the benefit of all the people of Canada and particularly the farm population because Conservative policies contain limitations that the policies of the former government did not contain.
We believe that the policies of the former government were correct policies. At the same time we admit that someone else could perhaps evolve better policies and if this could be done we are going to try to assist in putting them into effect because the people of this country, including the farm population, come first in the view of Liberals and the interests and well-being of Canadians are placed ahead of politics. Therefore, we would like to be as helpful as we can in seeing measures put into effect that will work to the benefit of all Canadians.
Hon. members of this house of the Liberal party have endeavoured to apply themselves to a search for effective farm policies. We enacted the Agricultural Prices Support Act which we endeavoured to implement to the best of our ability. Returning to my original premise that we must adopt policies that are in the best interests of Canadians from coast


to coast, I would point out that if we are going to have an effective and permanent farm policy it also must benefit all those engaged in the agricultural industry.
Many hon. members have risen in this house and said that the existing Agricultural Prices Support Act was helpful to the agriculture industry and superior to the proposed bill concerning agricultural stabilization. If that act contains principles that are of value and if there is any merit in the bill before us perhaps the government would give consideration to amalgamating parts of both measures. Instead of concentrating on the bill before us perhaps they would give consideration to bringing in a measure that would incorporate the best features of both the proposed bill and the existing act. The preamble to the existing Agricultural Prices Support Act stated that the farmer was entitled to receive a fair share of the national wealth. Although it may not have been achieved in any particular period nevertheless that was the objective of the act.
The bill before us refers to a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services they buy but makes no specific reference to the entitlement of farmers to receive a fair share of the national income. There is no guarantee of that in the bill before us nor is it stipulated as an objective of the bill. Perhaps we could combine the benefits of both measures in one piece of legislation.
I have observed that some hon. members in criticizing agricultural policies seek to compare the situation in Canada with the situation that obtains in other countries in relation to agriculture. I would suggest that there is no comparison between Canada and any other country. It is difficult to formulate a forward pricing system for Canada if the situation here is to be compared with that which obtains in importing countries.
Canada is capable of becoming the greatest exporting country in the world. We have proven this to be true as far as wheat is concerned and although it is not evident with respect to other farm products it could become so and it should be our ambition to have Canada become the greatest exporting country in the world. To the extent that we export we increase the national wealth of Canada. No matter how self-sufficient a country is there is no guarantee that the national wealth or standard of living will improve but if a country exports its national wealth increases by the value of its exports. Perhaps Canada's present national wealth can be attributed to her export activity. Therefore, I say that we should consider bills,

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
agricultural and otherwise, from the point of view of the situation in Canada.
In the matter of the export of wheat I know of no country that has a situation similar to that of Canada. This bill does not refer to wheat except as it applies to eastern Canada. We export 80 per cent of our wheat and no other country compares with ours.
I think what the government is trying to do is to find a solution without imposing production controls. I think that is the primary objective. Other countries have endeavoured to find a solution and have utilized production controls in their endeavours to assist the farmers or to make it possible for the farmers to have at least a fair share of the national wealth. What we are endeavouring to do is to establish production and give the farmers a fair share of the national wealth on the basis of the farmers being free to conduct their own production as they see fit. We are not recommending acreage control or production control and not too much emphasis has been given to that aspect of the question in the speeches that I have listened to in this House of Commons.
I was just a little surprised at this. I believe some of the farm unions of Canada have agreed that in order to prevent production running wild-as some great leaders of farm organizations have interpreted it-there would have to be some production controls. That would have to be done if an incentive price were established which would bring about a greater production than would be normally considered the annual contribution of the farmers. I was somewhat surprised at farm unions accepting the idea that we should have controls on production. This is contrary to what we hear in the House of Commons. The question is often asked here, so long as there are hungry people in the world why should there be production controls? Perhaps that sounds reasonable and is reasonable. If we are to feed the hungry people of the world and have unlimited production, then those same hungry countries of the world, if we can refer to them as such, will have to change their distribution attitude in regard to their acceptance of the surpluses of other countries and use them to offset their lack of production in their own countries to feed their own people.
I would say that everyone will agree that Canadians are prepared to feed every person on earth, but they are not prepared to have any of that food wasted when it is distributed so that the individuals who need it do not receive it. Distribution in those underprivileged countries will have to be reorganized before we can adapt ourselves to the position that, regardless of anything, we are going to supply all of the people that it is 96698-220
possible to supply with unlimited food and then depend on someone else to compensate us for the production of that food. Everyone has some interest in the production and distribution of this food throughout the world. I have not yet heard any individual or any country say that we can continue in season and out of season to produce something and give it away and still maintain ourselves in a solvent position. To the extent that it can be done of course it should be done.
If our farm unions have accepted the premise that in order to have parity prices for the farmers we must have production controls, if they are prepared to accept that, then it should be advocated on the same basis as it is in other countries where it has been established and the farmers should have the right to vote on it. We have been accepting the proposition of the organized farmers of western Canada and of all Canada. What about the unorganized farmers of this country? I hope I am not misstating the position when I say that the unorganized farmers in this country are perhaps in the majority. Who is speaking for them? They may have the same objective as the organized farmers; yet, I think they are entitled to a voice; not all the people who are working in industry are unionized. Would anyone say that the non-unionized individuals should not have a voice? Do members of parliament not represent, or try to represent, all of the people in their constituencies, organized or not? I think we try to present the point of view of all of the people in this House of Commons and all of them have a right to a voice in their affairs. We accept the voice of the organized farmers because we have no other particular voice to accept but at the same time consideration should be and will be given to the minority view. If the unorganized farmer is in the minority, he still has his rights as a member of that minority.
We are accepting the voice of the organized farmers of Canada and the basis upon which they think farm legislation should be enacted. I note that the 10 points offered by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture suggest to the government how a parity price structure should be enacted. The 10th point reads as follows:
Price supports should not create incentives to production which perpetuates surplus production problems and prevent necessary and desirable production adjustments being made.
To my mind this is the crux of the whole situation. How are you going to establish a parity basis? It certainly is desirable. How are you going to do it and still give consideration to point 10, which I think eliminates
3476	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization much of the argument in favour of establishing what some people advocate? It eliminates it because it all gets back to the question of how you can do the one thing without creating an undesirable situation in endeavouring to accomplish your objective. We have heard about the situation in the United States; we have heard about their parity or lack of it, and what it has done for the farmer-and it has helped the farmer. But they have never had parity in the United States. At the present moment I think they are advocating a reduction of the percentage parity to 65 per cent.
We have never had 100 per cent parity, or anywhere near it, although in some products or some commodities, at one time or another we may have had it. The price support mentioned in this bill is to be the average over a period of 10 years. I have compared the parity price in the United States during the last year, and the highest price was for hogs, and it was 92 per cent of parity. The lowest was for turkeys and barley, which was 61 per cent of parity. That was the situation in the United States and it created a surplus. The average price was 75 per cent of parity. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture point 10 suggests that a basis should be established which will not create production incentives. Where is the balance to be between the two? Farm leaders, and many prominent ones in Saskatchewan, have told us over the years that you cannot have a parity price above 75 per cent of parity. No one has explained to me why we should not have 100 per cent parity.
The farm organizations admit that if you are going to have 100 per cent parity you must have controls. They admit that. The farm people of this country should decide which they want. In my opinion, in a democratic country this decision should be made by a vote such as the farmers in the United States have before parity prices can be obtained on wheat or any other product. The farmers have a vote, and have a right to say whether they shall take parity with reduced production, reduced acreage, or whether they shall take whatever price the market offers on an unlimited production basis. I think that is democracy, and I really think that that should be done in this case.
I do not see how you can establish a ten-year average as the basis when that ten-year average is below the price that should prevail, and then establish a floor price of 80 per cent of that average without allowing the farmers to indicate their wishes in the matter. I do not believe, either, that the


basis of the price structure should be written into the law of the land. I have heard arguments in this house to that effect. Some people say, how can we depend upon the government to accept the recommendations of farm leaders of this country as to what the prices should be because the government may come along in an election year and raise that price. If that is the situation, then that is one of the prices that we pay for democracy.
I believe the government is responsible for conducting the affairs of this country, and is responsible for what happens to the national treasury. I do not believe that any group, whoever they might be, in any class or industry has the right to determine the things that the government itself should determine. I would say if we are going to adopt this measure then the farmers should have a part in it and should be prepared to accept the consequences, without putting the responsibility on any particular government that may have been in power at any given time. I feel, therefore, that we shall have to consider that.
As I mentioned before, many people on this side have been critical of the Conservative platform and critical of the Conservative party's promises before the election. I have explained why I thought the Conservatives were in the same position before June 10 as the splinter groups that are so vociferous in their criticism. Now that the Conservatives have formed the government I think it is the duty of Canadian people to endeavour to assist them. If referring this bill to the agriculture committee is going to be of any value, then of course that should be done.
However, I believe we are in a little different position now than we have been in former sessions of the house. I do not believe anyone will say that we have been deficient in having people advocate to the government or to the committees what should be done in this country. We have had the benefit of the advice of the farm groups in Canada. We have had the benefit of the advice of economists. If the government, in their wisdom, decide that this is the policy to follow, that this is what the farmers of this country want, that this is in the interests of all Canada, and if the government is accepting that responsibility, then I feel it is our duty to pass this bill. We are living in a democracy and elections come along from time to time. I do not believe the people of Canada are apt to be influenced in a way that some people are fearful they will be influenced. I cannot see that any

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
government would have any other objective than to try to do that which might be helpful to as many classes and producers in Canada as possible.
I believe that regardless of what the price structure may be, regardless, for instance, of what the floor price under eggs may be, it is absolutely essential, in order to make any price structure operative, that each one of the provinces accepts its responsibility. Living in Canada as we do, and having accepted our constitution as we have, I think it is impossible to make this price structure operative unless each province accepts its responsibility because the federal government can establish a 38-cent floor price under eggs but who is to guarantee that that floor price will accrue to the producer? The federal government cannot do that unless there is a change in the constitution, but the provincial governments can. I would say that some provincial governments have not been accepting their responsibilities.
I believe the day is coming when the people of this country are going to say, if everything is dependent on the federal government and the provincial governments are only to be distributing agencies for federal government revenue and be in a position where they can criticize to their hearts' content the efforts of the federal government, then what are we doing with provincial governments? I think this floor price structure can be made effective through provincial governments which could guarantee the farmer the floor price that the federal government establishes. There is room, therefore, for great co-operation throughout Canada.
I know of no argument that would be valid for referring this bill to the agriculture committee. Nevertheless, I would suggest that under present circumstances, with governments as they are constituted in Canada and with perhaps an uncertainty in the air about things to come, there may be some reason why the government would like to enact this legislation and present it to the country for its acceptance or rejection. Perhaps that is the way things should be done in our democracy. After all the cabinet and the government are responsible to the people; that is the way it should be. On that basis, I think I can support this bill, in the hope it can be improved and made effective, thereby giving some encouragement to the farmers of this country. The enactment of this legislation may give them hope that within a short time they will be entitled to their fair share of the national wealth.

When the minister moved second reading of the bill he made a very full and complete explanation of the measure as well as the amendments he intends to propose. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that many members do not understand yet the full significance of that explanation. speechtext:
I assume that the former minister has them all there. He generally has most figures fairly close at hand, and he makes the best use of them for his own purposes.
The hon. member for Melville also stated on more than one occasion during this debate that this stabilization bill does not differ from the price support act or that it is not even as good. To suggest that, Mr. Speaker, is to say that much more good could have been accomplished under the prices support act but "we didn't want to do it". That admission means a good deal, coming as it does from the previous minister.
The hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Villeneuve) made a very good speech last night. I want to add just a word to what he said with regard to cheese producers. On more than one occasion I have used the cheese producers in Ontario as an example of an organization which has tried to do its best for itself, in a self-help program under


the producer marketing board legislation. That organization has not always had the closest co-operation with the previous federal government. In some cases, as mentioned last night by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-and I will not repeat what he said -it would even suggest that there had been straight out and out antagonism toward what they were trying to do.
Last night the hon. member mentioned cheese imports in 1951 and 1952. It is not always our own production that causes the surplus position and causes us so much trouble but rather that which is imported from other countries on top of our own production. I suggest that at that time that was what caused the cheese producers more harm, worry and concern than anything that has happened in some time.
As stated last night by the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott, the cheese producers have cost this country only some $150,000 since the inception of that organization, in support in any way that is directly connected with their production. I am not referring to any buildings for cold storage and so on. But in the sale of their product, it has cost this government only some $150,000 in the years it has been operating. Any organization that can accomplish that result and do it themselves is to be commended very highly. Prior to that, however, I think the minister will recall that back in 1947 or 1948-I am not sure of the exact year but he will remember it very well-he lowered the subsidy on cheese producers milk or cheese milk from 10 cents to 8 cents and left it at 10 cents for all the other milk producers. That action had an effect upon the milk producers organizations of this country which it took a considerable number of years to heal. But in the case of these imports, surely Canadians should not be called upon to subsidize producers of another country.
The hon. member for Melville made much of the fact that we had changed this bill. Mr. Speaker, I hope that we on this side of the house will never take the attitude that we will not change our minds. If the hon. member for Melville and his cabinet colleagues had been willing to listen to those who knew the situation they might well have still been on this side of the house. Even with the last minute flurry of activity the previous government found that they had fiddled too long and their little Rome burned on June 10. It always intrigues me to hear so many who are not farmers tell us how we are supposed to run our business.
The hon. member for Melville also was crying crocodile tears the other day-you could almost hear them falling on the floor- and saying that we had joined with the C.C.F.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
party to defeat Liberalism. I am glad he has given us the assurance that they are not going to try the same thing. He also suggested that we had promised 100 per cent parity. Never at any time in our promises, our platform or policy did we ever suggest 100 per cent parity. We know the position in which the administration in the United States have been placed; and they have only 90 per cent parity, with surpluses beyond the reasonable point, and it is costing them a tremendous amount of money to pay the storage costs alone on those surpluses.
I have no hesitation in saying that the average farmer in Canada today is in practically the same position, netwise, as he was during the 1930's. We are trying now to do what we can to correct the situation but it cannot be done by one stroke of the pen. Although we feel that much can be accomplished under this legislation, we have never suggested that it could cure all of the problems of the agriculture industry. The prices to the producer for food products have not kept pace with wage increases over past years. Proof of that is in the fact that never before in the history of this country would the average industrial hourly wage buy so much food. I think that statement bears repetition-never before in the history of this country would the average industrial hourly wage buy so much too.
In a speech made in Ridgetown apparently on January 15, since the newspaper clipping I have in my hand is headed January 15, Dr. D. N. Huntley of the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph made this statement:
Whereas in Canada it takes only 30 minutes' work to earn enough money to provide an adequate diet for the average town worker, in the United States it takes 24 minutes, in Denmark 42 minutes, in Sweden 54 minutes, in Italy three hours and 12 minutes and in India four hours and 30 minutes.
Therefore the Canadian worker is not spending too much of his income on food.
We have heard quite a bit from the C.C.F. party about the wonderful governments they have in Sweden and Norway. I suggest that those figures show they are paying more in those countries for their food in comparison to what we have to earn for the same purpose in Canada. As I said before, net wise the farmer is nearly as badly off today as he was in the thirties and, after all, it is the net position which counts. He may have a lot of money in his pockets but if it takes him more money to keep going and he has less left over at the end of the year, then he is in a worse position. It is the cost-price squeeze that is catching him at this time.
The percentage of the consumer dollar going to the farmer is considerably reduced. Our government has set up a commission to try to find the details and causes of this
greater spread between the producer and the consumer. The primary producer bears the burden of increased taxation far out of proportion to his income by reason of the fact that he cannot pass on his costs to anyone else. He sells on a free market in most cases and buys on a protected market. During periods of recession and low prices he simply stops any improvement program, repairs old equipment rather than purchasing new and in most cases he is even forced to increase production in order to try to meet these higher costs.
How does this affect the rest of the economy? When one realizes that the average farmer buys between four and five times as much manufactured or processed goods as does the average urban dweller, then the possible effects on the merchant or the manufacturer are obvious. If the farmer across Canada received his fair share of the national income there would be very little unemployment. They are good spenders if and when they have it to spend.
Farmers ordinarily depend partly on increased real estate values for their retirement funds. There is no group of people who have, however, as much faith and hope in the future. That must have been pretty obvious to anyone sitting in the opposition over the last few years when these people would go on taking what they did take from the last government and still keep on voting for them.
History may serve its purpose at times but it is the present and the future to which we as a government are looking. I personally believe that producing marketing boards with a co-operative subsidiary to take surplus production off the market is the answer to most of our marketing problems. To work efficiently, however, these marketing boards must be organized on a national basis. The necessary legislation was provided in this house last year to permit producer marketing boards to operate in the interprovincial and export fields. They were also given the authority by order in council to collect a fee from each producer, commonly known as the equalization fee. There are those who term this an indirect tax.
Call it what you may, it is still the producer's own money and surely he can use it as he wishes. It is only another form of insurance, and there are plenty of precedents for such action. Critics of the producer marketing board legislation did not raise a hue and cry when the employees contributed to unemployment insurance to carry them over periods of unemployment. There was nothing said about a group of farmers getting together to set up a mutual fire insurance company.

Farmers' organizations generally are to be commended for their reasonable attitudes toward responsibility for surpluses. If this responsibility were divided between the producer and the government the possibility of unmanageable surpluses would be materially lessened. I would now like to quote from the brief of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture dated December 1957 which says in paragraph 10:
Price supports should not create incentives to production which perpetuate surplus production problems and prevent necessary and desirable production adjustments being made.
That is the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. In the case of the inter-provincial farm union council No. 3 of their recommendations states as follows:
Further in order to provide basic security to farmers guaranteed by legislation on agricultural commodities, the support market price should be established at levels sufficiently high to assure the consumer paying more than a disaster price, but not so high as to cause the government to accumulate large surpluses.
I would like to say again that I feel both farm organizations are to be commended for their reasonable attitude towards this matter of surplus production. As I mentioned before with respect to producer marketing boards, it will take considerable time and effort for producers across Canada to achieve the degree of organization which is desirable. The bill now before us will assist them in the meantime. At this point I would like to quote from the summary of the report of the royal commission on agricultural and rural life in Saskatchewan which, in conclusion No. 37 says:
A comprehensive agricultural program which gave agriculture bargaining power equal to other groups in the economy would reduce the need for a support price program. If the agricultural program is more limited and full employment and a high level of exports are not maintained, a support program is necessary. A support program would be desirable even if a comprehensive program were in force, although its operation would probably be limited to isolated marketing maladjustments.
And then conclusion 41 says:
Although farmers feel that the basic problem of low and variable farm income can be partly alleviated through lower costs of production, they feel the most fruitful program lies in the field of farm product prices and in finding larger markets for these products.
