Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I have no intention of unduly delaying the house nor do I wish to set myself up as an expert in agriculture. However, even if in certain parts of northwestern Quebec there is nothing but mines, lumber camps, or pioneer settlements, I am convinced that agriculture has a very important role to play there. That is why I feel called upon to state the views of the farmers, not only those of the constituency of Villeneuve, but also those of every area in northwestern Quebec. I do this even though my colleague, the member for Chapleau (Mr. Barbes) will also certainly have occasion to speak on behalf of the same farmers.
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I received several representations in the form of resolutions passed by the convention of the Catholic Farmers' Union of Temiscamingue, a federation of which several parishes of my constituency are members.
I do not doubt either that those resolutions meet with the wishes of every farming community in northwestern Quebec. Most of the resolutions passed by this convention, which took place at St. Eugene de Guigues, dealt with matters of topical interest in agriculture and were of interest not only to the farmers of our district but to all farmers in eastern Canada.
Among other things, this convention asked for a 10 cents a pound subsidy for butter, deficiency payments for agricultural products, a permanent federal policy of assistance to grain transport and also a permanent federal policy of agricultural price support. Improved methods for the grading of certain products were also requested.
In this brief which was prepared after the congress and which I believe must have been forwarded to the minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) it is interesting to analyse the content of the resolution requesting deficiency payments, since this is directly related to the bill now before the house.
To justify this request for deficiency payments the convention emphasizes the fact that in certain farming areas it is practically impossible to change over from one type of production to another in a short time. There are various reasons for this, depending on the type of production, the type of soil or the matter of marketing.
The convention also pointed out, and with good reason, that, like everybody else, the farmer is entitled to a certain stability of income, which is by no means insured by the sole method now applied, agricultural price support.
The farmer's convention also expressed the belief that the present agricultural price support policy should be supplemented by a system of deficiency payments negotiated at the end of a period where price levels would justify the adoption of such a policy, i.e. in the following circumstances:
1.	When the marketing of some perishable products has to be speeded up to prevent undue losses.
2.	When, in order to insure a better return to the producer, it would be necessary to raise a support price which has already reached its highest possible level, without further increasing an already surplus production.
3.	When it becomes necessary to supplement the inadequate income of producers who marketed their product at a price which
3482	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization remained dangerously low for two consecutive years, or when some factors, such as the incapacity to deliver the product or other particular circumstances, require the implementation of such a policy.
4.	When in certain particular cases, such payments provide a price support-allowing for special consideration to consumer interests-or ensure a steady supply, or solve any other marketing problem.
I believe that the requests embodied in the resolution passed by our farmers at their convention last fall, are justified and sound, and that is why I would like to call the governments attention to their contents today.
As I said a few minutes ago, I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that agriculture is playing a very important part in western Quebec. I made this statement because we have in our district more than 9,500 organized farms covering over 300,000 acres, and valued at least at 55 million dollars. We have to admit that the industry whose gross product exceeds $11 million a year is certainly a decisive factor in the prosperity and stability of our regional economy.
In northeastern Quebec the dairy industry is the only one in which our farmers are perfectly organized. No wonder farmers try to bank on it for the major part of their income. In fact, dairy production in that area, which amounted to 99 million pounds in 1941 was in excess of 150 million pounds in 1955. As a result, our farmers rely especially on butter production for their main income, because they find it very difficult, nowadays, to engage in livestock production, for distribution facilities are not as good as one might wish. Our farmers have to ship their beef either to Montreal or Toronto, because there are no slaughtering and cold storage facilities in our area. Therefore, they have to rely almost entirely on dairy production and, as stated earlier by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) when speaking to the resolution, the support price of butter, at 58 cents a pound, is not high enough to allow a reasonable profit to our farmers.
I believe that a program of deficiency payments, so that consumers would not have to pay exorbitant prices, would help farmers who want to stay on the farm in producing a commodity which the consumer could afford and which, at the same time, would provide the farmers with a reasonable profit.


That is why I endorse the suggestions made by our farmers who are members of the Union Catholique des Cultivateurs and who met in convention last fall more particularly to acquaint us with their needs.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on this subject of farm assistance, I wish once again to draw the attention of hon. members who, from time to time, have chosen to draw comparisons between farming and various other industries. For instance, an hon. member contended that through the Gold Mine Assistance Act the government was appropriating considerable sums of money to help mining. Well, the farmers who are asking for help from the Canadian government at this time are precisely those who take advantage of the Gold Mine Assistance Act. They are the same farmers because if that industry slows down or in wiped out, farmers in northwestern Quebec and northwestern Ontario are going to be the ones to feel it, since their only markets are in those mining areas where not only gold but essential base metals such as copper, lead, zinc and so on, are produced. I therefore believe that appeals to the Canadian government for help to Canadian farmers should not be based on that type of reasoning.
Mr. Speaker, I would also draw the government's attention to the difficulties which some of our farmers are facing in the distribution of their products, more particularly in our area. I may be told that this is a matter coming under provincial jurisdiction, but did not the previous government ask the Senate to set up a special committee to study land use? Would it not be possible to do the same thing? It is not only by enacting legislation such as the one before us today that we can really help the farmers and allow them to enjoy a better share of our national revenue; another way of doing it would be to revise methods which are now outdated.
I do not wish to take any more of the time of the house. I hope therefore that the hon. Minister of Agriculture will study this matter together with the provinces in seeking means to ensure better distribution of agricultural products, thus helping our Canadian farmers. (Text):

Mr. Speaker, I submit that these distressing conditions changed very little during the 22 years the Liberals were in office, and I do not think the Canadian people expect that in six months time these conditions are going to be changed. I want to emphasize that these conditions are getting worse. I happen to represent at least part of 14 rural municipalities in this parliament. The Moose Range municipality is partly in Mackenzie and partly in Prince Albert. I have not a division of the list of people in arrears for taxes according to where they reside, but hon. members will probably be interested in knowing that arrears of taxes in this municipality have gone up from $89,000 five years ago to $306,000 at the end of 1956.
I have a list here of the farmers in the municipality who are in arrears for taxes. This list is posted in the elevators so that the farmers have to make some adjustment on their taxes before they can get any cash from the sale of grain. There are over 800 names on this list. There are 29 farmers who are owing over $1,000; there are 90 who are owing between $500 and $1,000. There are many who are owing $200, $139 and $347. I am sure the Prime Minister considers some of these people as his friends. They gave him very good support on election day. I am sure it is not because these people are dishonest that they are in this position where their arrears of taxes now total over $300,000. It was because of the agricultural policies which were put in force by the previous government that a great many farmers in all parts of Canada were placed in this position. However, Mr. Speaker, I think we cannot let the present government escape the fact that it gave the Canadian people the impression that it had diagnosed the symptoms and prepared a remedy.
The present Prime Minister in opening his campaign in Massey Hall on April 25, 1957, was reported in the press as saying:
We will assure the farmer of his fair share of the national income by maintaining a flexible- and I underline the word "flexible"-price support program to ensure an adequate parity for agricultural producers based on a fair price-cost relationship. I will go into that on another occasion. It represents in general the viewpoint of organized agriculture across Canada.
He did not say 80 per cent; he said parity. Speaking in Minnedosa, Manitoba on May 16, 1957 as reported in the Toronto Star the Prime Minister said:

Speaking at an afternoon rally in the Kipling recreation hall, the Progressive Conservative leader told the 400 persons present that the basic price of $1.40 now paid for wheat was too low, and in light of rising living costs, worth only 50 cents when compared with purchasing power in depression years.

When the cost of what the farmer has to buy is continuing to go up and the farmer's net income is going down our farm people are being placed in an impossible squeeze. I have just had

a letter in the mail today from one of my constituents who wrote on January 15. He said this:
First of all, the prices on the farm commodities are rotten. They are worse now than they were a year ago. I remember eggs a year ago were 31-32 cents a dozen. Today the same A large eggs are only 27 cents a dozen. While the price on things the farmer has to buy still mounts.
And he goes on to say that the farm outlook becomes worse and worse. I was a bit disturbed about the comments made by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Studer). Believe it or not, he and I were together for more than five weeks and we did not quarrel during all the time we were away. We agreed to leave our differences of opinion at home and to be as congenial as possible. I was at Bombay when the hon. member spoke for Canada when the first shipload of wheat was turned over to the people of Bombay. I was sorry that this afternoon his references implied that our generosity is not being handled properly. I am glad he did not make the comments he made here in parliament two or three years ago when a similar suggestion was up for consideration. However, I think it is unfair to the Canadian people even to throw out the suggestion that the very generous gifts that we have been sending there are not properly handled.
I think it is fairly obvious that India has not been a large importer. They are not able to unload grain as it is unloaded at Fort William, Churchill or Montreal. India does not expect to be an importer. This last year as a result of drought, they have had a reduction of about 25 per cent in their cereal crop, and they appreciate very much the fact that Canada is sending $7 million worth of wheat to prevent starvation. As I recall what the hon. member said in Bombay, he did not say that Canada would be prepared to help them in the future only if they made certain changes in the way in which they did things at home. He spoke as a very generous guest and mentioned the fact that we had large surpluses available. He said that as members of the commonwealth we were anxious to share our prosperity with them. I am sure he will correct me if I am interpreting what he said incorrectly. For him now to suggest that we are going to become a little bit tough, that we are going to ask the people of India to make some basic changes in the way they are doing things before we are going to continue our generosity is something that I think he should not do. I think as members of the commonwealth we must not lose sight of the fact that we are probably the most favoured section in all the commonwealth. Our per capita income is over $1,000 while the per

capita income in India is about $56. It is a little bit more in Ceylon and a little bit less in Pakistan. I think that Canada can afford to take some long-term risks.
I think all hon. members appreciated the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he said we are going to give an additional $15 million worth of wheat and that we are going to sell $35 million worth and give credit for a ten-year period. There was not a dissenting voice that I heard in parliament and I have not seen in the press any comments which suggest that Canada cannot do this. As a matter of fact the Toronto Telegram carried a front page story saying that this is going to provide prosperity from Halifax to Vancouver, that it is going to provide employment for the railways, to be good for the elevators and is going to get some money into the pockets of the farmers.
While I agree with the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek that Canada cannot hope to solve all the problems of the world, nevertheless while we are spending $5 million a day on our defence program I think we can dispose of some of our surplus products to these other countries. I think we must pay some attention to what is being done in other parts of the world. I think we could dispose of much larger quantities of surplus products in that part of the world if we were prepared to accept local currency and were prepared to give these people a chance to send some of their manufactured goods to Canada. But I think both the present government and the previous government created a great deal of ill-will throughout the world in complaining of what the United States was doing to try to prevent starvation. Instead of complaining about what the United States was doing I think we might have had a look at what the Minister of Trade and Commerce is now suggesting, namely that this year Canada will give away an additional $15 million and move another $35 million on a credit basis.
I think it is significant that Canadian farmers have been going farther and farther in debt under the Liberals and now under the Conservatives while farmers in other countries have been getting real help from their government. In "Agriculture Abroad" for December, which is published under the authority of the minister who is piloting this bill through the house, there is a section on what is being done in the United States. It says that farm incomes are increasing there for the second consecutive peacetime year, the only such increase since 1947. The figure on a per farm basis shows an increase from 1955 to 1956 of 7 per cent; prices received by farmers are 4 per cent above a year ago and the improvements have been
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization achieved primarily in the market and not through price support. Farm assets are at an all time high; exports of farm commodities total $4.7 billion in 1957 and are also at an all time high both from the point of view of quality and value.
There is also quite an interesting section on the soil bank program. In the October issue of this publication it refers to what the Tory government in Great Britain has been doing for the farm people of that country. There have been deficiency payments there and I am sure that when the wheat pool people come back to see the cabinet in order to discuss deficiency payments the minister will have in mind the fact that his own publication draws attention to the fact that deficiency payments in Great Britain have been carried on for some time. Their grain deficiency payments this year were $391 million compared with $74 million in the previous year; wheat subsidies were $50 million, $5 million higher than the previous year. Barley payments were $27 million compared with $24 million in the previous year. Total subsidies in the United Kingdom were $629 million compared with $551 a year ago.
Again in this publication "Agriculture Abroad" also in October, it says that the soil bank program in the United States had a limit beyond which no farmer could draw from the fund, namely $3,000. A great many Canadian farmers would be very glad if the Canadian government would say "If you will not seed any wheat, oats or barley on 100 acres of land we will pay you a maximum of $3,000." In some areas it might be $27 an acre but for 120 acres if you did not seed the government would give you the maximum amount that you could have.
There is a limit also in respect of farm conservation measures in the amount of $5,000. Therefore, when one considers that the whole Canadian economy has been bubbling over with prosperity for large corporations, and that when we were discussing the pipe line bill a couple of years ago the present Minister of Trade and Commerce mentioned there were some large fortunes being made and that Mr. McMahon, in one of his oil ventures was able to make something like $5,000 for every dollar he invested; and while our gross national product is at the highest level in Canada's hisory, it is unfortunate as so many members from various parties have indicated, that young and old people are leaving the farm, giving up the good life for which they have been trained to go to the city. In some cases they will join the ranks of the unemployed or they will try to qualify for something before they get any older. In pursuing this policy we are making a
3488	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization great mistake, especially in view of the fact that two out of every three people in the world are hungry. Yet the former and present governments have deliberately pursued policies in Canada preventing Canadian food from being produced and made available to these hungry people.
Our average life expectancy is 70 years of age and it is just half that in India and Pakistan. Yet we are members of the commonwealth; we believe in the common good. We nevertheless are starving our people off the farms saying we do not care whether they starve-we are going to carry out this policy.
A former major general of the Canadian army stated recently that Canada could cut its defence expenditure in half, that for $800 million we could have as good a defence as we now get for double that amount. I am not able to check the accuracy of his statement but I do think the policy which we worked out in this country during the war-that whatever was physically possible somehow must be made financially possible- is a policy which should be worked out now. Two out of every three people in this world are going hungry and a large section of our own brothers and sisters in the commonwealth have never had one good meal. The very limited amount of assistance we have given them has offered them some hope but one must remember that a country like Germany, defeated by us in war, is able to pay its farmers $2.70 per bushel to produce wheat; Italy, a relatively poor country, is able to pay $3.60 to wheat growers; the Netherlands pays $1.92 and Switzerland, $3.73. These countries, as part of their national program, are able to use public funds to ensure that those who till the soil and plant the seeds, who run the risks of weather conditions, should have something like a fair share of the national economy.
I hope the minister will reconsider over the week-end the proposal of the hon. member for Moose Mountain so that he can have firsthand information from the representatives of farm organizations and also from the unorganized farmers who may attend before such a committee and tell us some of the facts of life.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may as representative for the constituency of Gaspe and a member from the province of Quebec, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) for introducing his bill No. 237 entitled "an act to provide for the stabilization of prices of agricultural commodities".


This measure was greeted enthusiastically by all farmers of the province of Quebec as a guarantee for them as far as the price of their products is concerned for the future.
I would not want to hold the attention of this house too long and repeat what has already been said by my colleagues on the advantages of this bill. However, I should like to remind the house that, among farmers of my constituency, there is a class of people which has been too long forsaken and which surely deserves the attention of the house. I am referring to the settlers of my area.
In my constituency, there are many settlements whose population is made up of honest people who perpetuate the contribution made here in this country by our pioneers. These people go on clearing the land, pushing back the forest, increasing the number of farms; I believe, Mr. Speaker, that these agricultural pioneers deserve our consideration. For that reason I am proud to speak on their behalf and to defend their cause. No section of the community has been more neglected than these poor settlers who are meeting with serious difficulties in bringing up their families. Their day's work starts early in the morning and ends late at night.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that these people will get their share of the amounts appropriated under this legislation and I am confident that the government will add pulp-wood to the products specified in the bill. When adding it to this classification, I believe special consideration should be given to the first 25 cords cut in the year because, as you no doubt know, these people have to sell their wood at the ridiculous price of $8 or $9 a cord and to accept the price they are offered because they must support themselves and their families.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, those people are refused the benefits of several beneficent measures passed by this government and even by the former government. It is my duty to point out that farmers who cut pulpwood on their farm-not as much for business purposes as for the purpose of clearing their land, sometimes in the course of the winter have to go and work as woodcutters for certain companies. There are some in my constituency who were employed by the Gaspesia Sulphite Company at Chandler. While they were thus employed they accumulated in their books a certain number of unemployment insurance stamps. They therefore went back to their own farms and proceeded to cut pulpwood in order to clear their

land. This pulpwood was exactly the same type as that which they had been cutting for the company. They sold it to the same company. And yet, as far as cutting wood on their own farms is concerned, they have no right to unemployment insurance stamps, though they had contributed to the unemployment insurance fund when they were cutting wood for the company.
I believe that these people certainly deserve the attention of the house and that it is my duty to acquaint my colleagues with their position.
Mr. Speaker, I will not spend any more time on the subject. I am confident, however, that I will obtain the approval of every hon. member who, like me, takes an interest in this type of settler.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage I would like to offer a few remarks which I feel will be of some use to the people of Chapleau which I represent in this house and which number more than
41,000	people directly interested in agriculture.
On December 11, 1957, in committee, the house passed a resolution introducing a bill guaranteeing support prices for certain agricultural products. That is Bill No. 237 at present under discussion.
Any product which the government may wish to designate will be supported by the proposed measure. On that score I am certainly of the opinion of the hon. member who spoke before me, the member for Gaspe (Mr. English), who went so far as to request that the settlers from the Gaspe peninsula, and therefore the settlers of any area whatever, should benefit from this measure with regard to pulpwood. However as far as I am concerned, I rather wish to speak only of agriculture. I will therefore continue on that subject.
A board made up of three members and an advisory committee made up of from 6 to 9 members will see to the administration of the act. The funds are available to the government for the benefit of agriculture, and under the former legislation, of course, we already had a $200 million fund available to the Agricultural Prices Support Board.
The government now wants to stabilize to a greater extent the income of our farmers by setting base prices established by calculating the average for the ten previous years.
What the farm population is mostly interested in, in my opinion, is to know whether the cost of production, in relation to income,
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization leaves to the farmers a profit which is sufficient to give more prosperity to the farm.
The government suggests that all farm commodities should come under support prices, except for wheat, oats and barley, which are already covered by some other legislation.
Mr. Speaker, there is a large farm population in my area and we had hoped for a bill providing for more equitable prices for those who earn their living in clearing and tilling new land.
On November 8, 1957, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) had suggested to the house that it was urgent to discuss the legislation aimed at improving the agricultural situation. To that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) had replied that we were just trying to get a little bit of publicity.
Personally, on October 29, I expressed in this house my earnest hope to see the passing of legislation specially beneficent to farmers of eastern Canada.
On December 2, 1957, the leader of the government in this house announced the business of the house for the next day and said that item number 116 on the day's order paper under government notices of motions would be taken up.
Nothing has been done during that period and yet, since the 31st of October we had been waiting for an agricultural policy which had been promised for years and which was going to bring prosperity to agriculture as a whole.
Today, our workers cannot find employment as easily as they think they should. Farmers' earnings are inadequate. Instead of finding customers for their goods, merchants are forced to take them back. This goes for farm machinery, trucks and all kinds of vehicles.
In June 1957, voters in such agricultural districts as Abitibi and the Gaspe peninsula were repeatedly told by the Conservatives that they would enjoy greater prosperity under a conservative government. They waited for this to take place, and instead of introducing active measures in 1957 to increase the income of the settlers, the Conservatives left the farmer, the pioneer, to his fate.
Now, on April 8, 1957, the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, spoke in favour of a national conference on agriculture which would be held as soon as he was in power. I quote from page 3263 of Hansard of April 8, 1957. The then leader of the opposition said:
. . . we believe that the time has come when, in the interests of the national welfare of agriculture, a national conference on agriculture should
3490	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization be convened. This would be representative of the federal and provincial governments and of farm organizations with the responsibility of suggesting a general policy for domestic and international trade so as to assure the farmer a fair and proper share of the national income and also permit farmers to have a part in formulating policies for the promotion of the welfare of agriculture.
Then, this fall, in 1957, when the government introduced Bill No. 14 to help western farmers market their grain, the farmers of Chapleau were concerned over the stand of the present Prime Minister and we repeatedly asked for prompt action and immediate steps to help agriculture. We are still sorry to see that the present Conservative government has failed to enact the efficient legislation which it dangled before the eyes of Canadian voters last spring, when Liberals in particular were being blamed, and when tears were being shed over the predicament of farmers whose production costs for hogs were $41 a hundred pounds while the support price was but 23 cents a pound. As can be seen on page 1402 of Hansard, under the new government, imports of pork from the United States for the month of August alone, reached 377,241 lbs., if you please. And when will our farmers in the Abitibi see all those promises materialize that were made to them by the Conservatives? We do not know yet.
Together with the farmers, we could wish for new action, for new developments on the part of this government, at least since October last.
The hon. Prime Minister of today has, without any reservation, advocated collective marketing of farm products. The farmer is squeezed between rising costs and falling prices. When in western Canada, the need of the grain producers was recognized, those people were voted credits, and even advance payments. The Conservatives held out before the people in our constituencies a revision of price supports, as well as quick legislation to help the farmers first to survive and then to reach a decent standard of living. Well, the time has come, and it is only fair that I should be the spokesman of thousands of families in Abitibi and elsewhere.
According to the 1956 census, in Quebec we have 122,617 farms, and we want the government to achieve something to get results, in view of its so bombastic program announced in the spring of 1957. The people from the prairies got ahead of us, Mr. Speaker, in the first two weeks of the session. So we have been seeking action since the end of October, and we should like to have practical measures that would give tangible results.

Our farmers today, not only in Chapleau but in eastern Canada, are receiving less and paying more. In saying this, I am not saying anything new to the government, because the leader of the Conservative party, now Prime Minister, claimed the same thing in April, May and June 1957.
Let the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hark-ness) delay no longer to correct this unfavourable situation in which the farmer finds himself. What has happened is not so much that selling prices have gone down, but rather that production costs have gone up at least 20 per cent.
The average income of farmers is not equivalent to that of other economic groups in this country. The Conservative party boasted to the electors that they should soon stabilize and balance agriculture. But the farmer, Mr. Speaker, is in no position to wait for such half-measures as investigations, etc. The vice-president of the Catholic Farmers' Union was perfectly right in stating at the annual convention of the Amos federation, held at Macamic, on September 24, 1957, that the fate of agriculture is at this time in the hands of the farmers themselves.
As for us, we cannot overemphasize this point. In view of the interdependence which exists between those who work on the farms and those who are employed in other activities or services, the government must stabilize agriculture to protect the Canadian economy.
For six months now, workers, small business men, salesmen and all the other working people have been affected by the delaying tactics of this government.
The Conservative party has been saying for a long time that it could improve the lot of our farmers. May I recall here that in 1941 the present Prime Minister, then a private member, boasted that he could quickly improve the position of Canadian agriculture. As early as the 23rd of March, 1953 he held that parliament should act immediately and directly, without any recourse to an investigation commission.
In the spring of 1957 the gentleman who is now Prime Minister of this country suggested that measures would be taken immediately and that there had been far too much delay already.
Mr. Speaker, if we consider the fact that the purchasing power of the dollar which was

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
100 cents in 1939 and which is approximately half that figure at this time, according to the price of those products used to figure up the cost of living index, we will understand how it is increasingly urgent to act, because of that fact as well as to make good election promises with regard to family allowances.
In the spring of 1957 the Conservatives claimed that farmers were headed towards economic depression. After the new government which was supposed to devise a cure-all for workers and farmers in particular has been in office for six months things are taking a turn for the worse, at least in my county. Well, is it not normal for us to ask that the wallet which before the general election of 1957 was said to be so full be opened wide for agriculture?
Eastern farmers are now anxious to be placed on the same footing by the right hon. Prime Minister as the prairie grain producers.
In Chapleau, my riding, the Catholic Farmers' Union had an investigation made at the end of last June into the main problems of farmers and on the pattern to be set in the agriculture of our area to insure its survival and expansion.
It has been found once again that agriculture today cannot provide a family with a decent living. In spite of such hard work on land sometimes difficult to farm, the desirable comfort is lacking.
About July 15, 1957, a delegation from Ontario and Quebec was received by the Minister of Agriculture; Mr. J. B. Lemoine, the general president of the U.C.C. made representations on behalf of the farmers and particularly of the dairy industry. One had really the impression that the delegates knew that the new government was more interested in promises than in new and advantageous policies.
What are the new and efficient measures offered by this government?
It has set up a royal commission. Well, Mr. Speaker, the eastern farmers, after seven months of stagnation, are still wondering what improvements are forthcoming to increase their well-being, as has been promised to them.
On the one hand, the farmer must succeed in cutting down his costs for a particular product by the use of new methods. It is a matter of internal economy and farmers are well aware of it.
On the other hand, they require that the government apply a price support policy which will be a stabilizing factor in normal times and a safeguard in periods of emergency. Organized farmers have already expressed their recommendations along those
lines. At their recent conventions, they have asked when the new government which was elected on glowing promises, will implement the safeguard of price support, when it will assist settlers and farmers in areas less favoured by the climate, so that they may enjoy a more attractive and more equitable standard of living.
Order in council 1632, dated December 10, 1957, established a commission. It is a good thing that experts such as Mr. Romeo Martin, president of the co-operative council of Quebec, have been appointed on this advisory committee of the government. But farmers had realized for many years that the present Prime Minister had confidently undertaken that, if he ever became the head of the country, he would at once apply some legislation, that would have to be adopted by Parliament, so that the new government could bring prosperity to farming families. Instead of that, we are to have now a stabilization board replacing the farm prices board. It is merely a change in name.
Having seen with what satisfaction many of our farmers had welcomed the promises made last spring, we were impartially expecting those efficient means that would spread prosperity such as had never been enjoyed in our farming areas. But we are to have only more surveys and, as for the rest of the question, the promises have brought nothing of direct benefit to our farmers. They will have to compete with the western farmers, under a less generous climate, and with regrettably higher transportation costs that are directly reflected in production costs, in view of the high prices asked for anything the farmers want to buy, like oats, for instance, or bran, or mill-feed and so on.
Our markets are often at a great distance, some lands are poorer, the climate does not change. Our people are still waiting for the results of an investigation on price spreads, instead of getting the new legislation that was announced with such great flourish for months and years, and which was to give a new drive to our agriculture.
According to the Conservatives, everything was dull and grey for our farmers before June 10. Everything was to become rose-coloured after the general election.
The Conservatives got the roses and the votes, and it is now up to them to pull out the thorns and to distribute the scented harvest amongst the farmers in the east as well as in the west.
It should be noted that before June, 1957, the Conservative candidates promised higher prices, a golden age to be introduced by them who blamed us for extravagance and overtaxation.
3492	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
I have even heard a roads department engineer, just imagine, urging us to vote for Mr. Diefenbaker who would, immediately after his election, raise the price of hogs from 23 cents to 41 cents a pound. Our friends from Chapleau are still awaiting the promised gift. What does the government intend to do for our less favoured areas such as the Abitibi district, the Gaspe peninsula and the Lake Saint John district where the soil is poorer and the weather more severe and where higher transportation costs add to the burden of the farming people? Nothing new, Mr. Speaker. Through trickery the Conservatives have grabbed a few honours and a few positions, while the farmers are left holding the bag with their conventions, their requests or their resolutions.
So if the new government is incapable of keeping its promises, let it at least bring in one quite urgent measure which was actually mentioned on October 14, on the first day of this present session. To bring help all at once to a whole agricultural area, agreement should be negotiated with the provinces in order to carry out with them a forestry development such as the one I am requesting at this time for the constituency of Chapleau, that is to say the industrial development at Mattagami.
In northwestern Quebec pulpwood is one of the most important agricultural products of this region and a specialized union of the Catholic Farmers' Union is still actively occupied with the marketing of this agricultural product which, in our constituency, is of primary importance.
Mr. Speaker, in the early days of May, 1956 a well-known Montreal newspaper, he Devoir, carried the announcement by the province of Quebec, through its leader, of an 80 or 100 million dollar project concerning the agricultural mining and forestry basin of Mattagami in my constituency. It was the promise of a large industry which was to create an unlimited market for an agricultural product, namely pulpwood, which is sold at a low price at this time while cost of transportation to markets are getting higher. It seems we are still waiting for federal assistance such as was proposed by this government on October 14 last. No concrete results have come out so far of this federal-provincial co-operation, at least as far as Quebec is concerned, and it will soon be two years since this project was announced on the front page of the newspaper referred to.
This is a concrete example of a case where the government could find a new way of helping the farmer of this part of the prov-


ince of Quebec called Abitibi. It would be a new factor of stabilization and sustained prosperity for agriculture because it would effectively solve the lack of employment which means hardship for everyone. The government would thus promote circulation of goods, salaries and markets for natural or processed products of agriculture-as they are called in this bill-and farm commodities would thus have a consumers' market which would be a local factor of price support and a factor of employment and adjustment in a country which needs them.
To achieve progress it is not enough to hold conferences and implement resolutions adopted by an advisory committee. In devising concrete solutions to farm problems, due account should be taken of the interdependence which is said to exist between farmers and other workers.
Under section 2, paragraph 2, of this act, it is proposed that the governor in council will take into consideration production costs and such other factors as he deems relevant. Let me mention here the cost of transportation, as one such factor, also the harsher climate and the transportation costs to distant markets. The production cost is the most significant to my mind, and it will be necessary for the government's advisers to consider local and regional conditions in the various farming districts.
To start out and to make good on our lands, the young settler must take the trouble to clear and enlarge his acreage. The first operations comprise pulpwood production, which is our first farm product.
I therefore wish to draw the attention of the government to the fact that, as far as my district is concerned, there is a very efficient way to help agriculture become more profitable and stable, and it is to associate with agricultural work the development of resources which will take this natural product of our land, pulpwood, and transform it into finished products. This must be done through federal-provincial co-operation. I have stated a very definite case where the provincial government seems to be prepared already to accept the federal aid which should be granted, if we are to go by the suggestions of October 14, 1957, made in this house, for the development of Canada in the district I have the honour to represent. Our farm population is even more considerable than the figure of 41,000 I gave a moment ago, for this is but half of the total population of my constituency; but everyone in my con-

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
stituency is interested in this vital problem, because we are all interdependent and we stick together.
Dealing as we are with the matter of adequate prices for farm products, I suggest that at the same time the government extend its consideration to a factor which is essential to the progress of our agriculture, and that is the combined agricultural and industrial development of our area so as to make sure that our agriculture as a whole will enjoy lasting benefits. At first, in our area, farming land yields pulpwood, our main product. I hope that the government will speed up its action and that it will not be content to repeat its promises which are slow to bear fruit. Farm products, including pulp-wood, should receive the attention of the government. This, in my opinion, is quite an urgent matter. When is this government going to achieve the objective so often referred to both before and after the election, namely put agriculture, generally speaking, in a position to yield to those engaged in it a material reward comparable to the one received by the other economic groups in Canada?
At Mont Tremblant, around September 18, 1957, at the congress of the Canadian producers of agricultural chemical products, the Minister of Agriculture advocated a more intensive use of fertilizers and favoured additional labour and machines. We are in agreement with him on that point, and if the government considers that agriculture is important, it should then help also those areas where farming is more difficult because of the climate or the land; that is what has already been proposed elsewhere in poorer areas of our country.
Under such conditions, farming will remain an important part of our economy and a factor of prosperity in our areas.
At this time agriculture owes its best results to the work of groups like the Catholic Farmers' Union and those professional associations which have brought to the farmers their most important victories. Today the Catholic Farmers' Union, as Mr. Lemoyne has so relevantly expressed it, wants the government to co-operate with its members in order to reorganize the development of agrarian resources and to create self-sustaining economic units.
All that would be very beneficial to our farming industry, and that is what we favour in order to get more vigorous and quick
action in launching industrial developments which will indirectly assist our farmers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I
will only speak for ten minutes or so.
At the resolution stage of this bill I offered certain criticism which I believed necessary at the time. I pointed out that the only guarantee provided by the bill was that the price of certain agricultural products could not be less than 80 per cent of the selling price based on the average price for the three preceding years. That was true at that time. However, since that date the formula has been changed and the 80 per cent base will now be established on the ten year average of the selling price. This amendment, I think, is an excellent improvement since this ten year period which will henceforth serve to establish the average includes a few years where the level of the selling price was far above that which it has reached over the three preceding years. This will therefore serve to improve to that extent the base price of 80 per cent.
Nevertheless, there remains the fact that instead of being based on production costs this average is to be based rather on the selling price. We know that for certain years at least a certain number of products were sold under their cost price. It will therefore be understood that this formula will bring the ten year average price to an inadequate level. I will admit that the base price is only a minimum and that it might well be adjusted to the advantage of the farmer by the addition of a certain percentage to the same base price which will become the price prescribed by the present bill. But all this is dependent on the goodwill of the government and on the co-operation of the minister who is entrusted with the administration of the act. At this level, there is admittedly a possibility of serious mistakes in spite of good intentions and in spite of a clause of the bill providing that in establishing a percentage of the base price the governor in council must take cost of production into account.
However, notwithstanding the restrictions I just pointed out, things could go on fairly well as far as the products listed in the bill are concerned. However, those are not the only ones which should be listed and I am wondering how they will go about it when the time comes to designate new products. Of course the governor in council will have this power but he is sometimes hard of hear-

I therefore ask the minister, when in committee, to add two products to the list of those he designated in his bill. I refer to pulpwood and maple syrup sold by farmers. The question was so well dealt with by the hon. members I just mentioned, particularly as regards pulpwood, that there is no need for me to deal with it at any length. As regards maple syrup, I dealt with that quite at length on December 11 last and I would only be repeating, perhaps for the tenth time, what I have already said if I were to deal with that product again. I do wish to point out however that those products, particularly maple syrup, represent two of the most important sources of income, at least for the farmers of Beauce, as this constituency is the most important producer of that product in the whole of Canada.
This price support measure contains nonetheless some prospective dangers which must be prevented at all cost unless we agree to head blindly for possible disaster. There is especially the danger of overproduction to which I myself referred when I spoke on the resolution. It is a trap towards which price parity seems to have led the agricultural economy of our neighbours to the south who now seem belatedly concerned about it.
I believe we must visualize the same situation concerning at least some of the commodities which are now mentioned in this bill, or other products which might be designated later on by the governor in council.
With regard to butter, I see no danger of overproduction. On the contrary, I maintain what I said on December 11 last, namely that our present supply of 33 million pounds is at a dangerously low level which must at all costs be raised for the protection not only of the producer but of the consumer as well. At this point, in fact, big business could to all intents and purposes gain control of that supply and hold it back for a while, thus creating an artificial shortage which would bring the price to a prohibitive level quite


unfair to the consumers, and without the producer getting any profit out of it.
The public still remembers, because it was the victim of this state of affairs, the speculation carried out over the winter of 1951-1952 when butter was being sold at 85 cents and even 90 cents a pound. It seems to me that to set this price at 63 cents, and even at 65 cents at the producer level, would be the best guarantee against a return of these inhuman practices, while doing away with any danger of overproduction.
However, as far as hogs and cattle are concerned, I think on the contrary that there will be danger of overproduction whenever a reasonable price is fixed for the producer. I will not venture to say with any certainty at all what should be the price set for cattle, not having the knowledge nor the information necessary in that regard. However, as far as hogs are concerned, I will say that 26 cents per pound for grade A animals should be a reasonable price which will allow the average producer a small profit. However, without this guarantee I will predict overproduction within twelve months or eighteen months. Does this mean that the remedy would then consist merely in again lowering the price to 23 cents a pound? It would be utterly foolish to do so, because, in that case, the small producer could not stand up and would necessarily lose out to the large cattle raiser who would find a way to protect himself against such difficulties.
I humbly submit that the solution would be the suggestion I made previously, whereby the number of heads the same producer could deliver to the board in a given period would be limited. It should be noted that such a procedure would in no way restrict production. Thus the small producer, who most deserves consideration, would be guaranteed a proper return for his labour. Furthermore, this procedure would discourage the large cattle raiser who does not need this kind of operation to make a living and who shows interest in it only so long as it can make large profits which are necessarily based on a large scale production. I am firmly convinced that such a procedure would eliminate the congestion of the market. And the same procedure could be applied to the cattle raising industry, after a suitable price has been established.
I would apply the same solution to the problem of pulpwood providing, however, the government agrees, which I doubt, to include this commodity among those which are going

How many cords of pulpwood could each producer deliver to the board each year? It would be foolhardy to venture a figure. The number of cords should be determined after a thorough study of the problem; it could even differ from one section of the country to another. But if we stop to study more particularly the case of this product, we find characteristics which are encountered in no other section, and I wish to mention that large producers of butter, cheese, pork and beef products as well as maple products, do not generally grow the raw material they use; they procure such material from numerous producers who are essential to them and who become therefore their indispensable associates.
In most cases, the situation is reversed as regards pulpwood for in this case there are big producers who, as a general rule, own the raw material used in their mills and could probably, for a certain number of years at least, do without the quantities they buy from small producers, if the price of their products increased too much. In fact, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, for example, in these last few years, less than 25 per cent of the pulpwood used by large mills has been supplied by settlers or farmers.
Without being an expert, I would venture to say that I see a possible remedy to such a dangerous situation even if it does not come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. This remedy could be applied at another level. Most of the great pulpwood companies which own timber land are merely lessees of crown property. Therefore provincial governments could probably prevent permit holders from using crown timber unless they have first bought the wood supplied by farmers and settlers. I am simply submitting this suggestion in the hope that experts, at the provincial level, will study and uphold it if it should prove practical and will reject it if it cannot be implemented.
However, if my suggestion is not practical, a better one will have to be found; otherwise, the board will likely have to go through hours of anxiety in the face of a surplus of timber for which it will be unable to find any buyer.
In any event, in spite of handicaps and difficulties-it is under such conditions, in my view, that the real value of the members of a government can be measured-we must at all cost include now or very soon in this bill farmers' and settlers' pulpwood. It is one of the conditions of the survival of farmers in eastern Canada.
Mr. Speaker, my statement on Bill 237 has been very incomplete and imperfect. I would be glad however if it helped to improve a bill which is considered as rather important by the farmers of the Beauce area and which I will support with my vote in spite of some rather serious weaknesses.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think that I can let this bill go through and the present amendment be voted on without saying something. I represent an agricultural constituency which was paid a little bit of attention in the last election by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I feel that I should have something to say about it. I am rather proud of this agricultural constituency which I represent, not only because it can be regarded as an agricultural constituency but also because it is somewhat diversified. As well as the larger portion of it being agricultural-we regard ourselves as a very strategic wheat-growing area-at the same time the area runs right slap up against the boundary of British Columbia and in the foothills of the Rocky mountains is a vast cattle country. In the south toward the east we have sugar beets and in the foothills toward the north we have the Turner valley oil fields. Then to the south and west we have the coal mining industry of the Crows-nest pass. That is a very nice constituency to represent. It is diversified enough for one to apply this study to the various problems which make it interesting.
However, regardless of that nice constituency, I speak on this measure because it has largely a farm population. Having a farm population, most of the small communities are dependent upon the farm income. The small towns that lie in the midst of the wheat-growing area are entirely dependent upon the farm income. In the town in which I live, namely the town Vulcan, there is a population of only about 1,500 but we have 10 double elevators in that community. A great deal of money passes

That characterizes the situation in wheat growing communities throughout the entire three prairie provinces.
I will not indulge in repetition. I have my own views as to the present amendment and many speakers in our group are very experienced farmers who know the agricultural business and have studied the problems of the farmer. They know the serious plight of the western farmer at the present time- depressed prices, disparity of prices between what they get for their products and what they have to pay to live and to operate their farms. There are members of our group who have spoken and some who are still going to speak and they know all about these things.
I said at the commencement of my remarks that the Prime Minister paid special attention to my constituency during the election. He came down there and held quite a large meeting in the town of High River. He made special mention of the farmers' problems. Of course, that is good political business, to talk of the problems of the particular constituency which one is visiting. He made particular mention that if his party was elected to power they would surely do something for the farmers. He dealt at great length with his proposals to straighten out the disparity between the income of the farmers in the west and that of people in other industries.
He referred to this matter of parity. He criticized some of our speeches in this group last session when we discussed parity. He indicated we were not altogether justified in asking for 100 per cent parity, but he said: "There is a place for parity in our program; if you elect my government I will get down to Ottawa and see the farmer gets a new deal in this respect." What is this new deal? What is this great promise, this great proposal the present Prime Minister was talking about? Is it the sort of thing we have before us now. If this is the new deal, then it is going to be a sorry disappointment to the farmers of western Canada.
You know there is such a thing as bluff and I think if the farmers are being bluffed at all it is in the assumption that this new bill is going to take care of their problems.
I do not know what the actions of the present government over the past few months, running here and there, doing this and that, calling one conference after another and bringing down certain types of legislation which anyone could bring down if they had the money
[Mr. Hansell.l

to spend, are going to do to help the farmers' problems. It appeared that they were actually going to do something on behalf of the farmers, but I believe we have in Canada today what is perhaps one of the biggest bluffing governments this country has ever seen. That is my impression.
You can talk of parity. Parity in my view is a word which indicates a certain completeness. You either have parity or you do not; one or the other. According to statistics the farm income of this country has dropped by about 10 per cent during the last year. I have with me some notes on this matter which I believe are from the Financial Post although I do not know whether they were quoting from some other publication. They say:
Farm income shows an 8.6 per cent decrease in the first three quarters of 1957.
Of course this government was not in power all that time so their predecessors will have to take some blame for this condition. Most of the decline came from reduced wheat sales. The total income amounted to $638 millions; the cash farm income estimated for nine months of this year-being $1,847 millions-about 3 per cent below that of the previous year. Lower returns from cereals grown was the major factor in the decline.
The point is well taken that throughout 1957 our farm income dropped about 10 per cent. That is serious if you do a little bit of comparing. If a man has a job, for instance, and he gets a salary of say $200 a month-not much of a salary these days, but it is only an imaginary figure-and he finds when he picks up his cheque one month that he is 10 per cent short, or $20 short, he is going to feel that something surely is wrong somewhere. That is the picture with respect to farm income over the last year.
We had reason to expect the farmers of the west were going to receive a better deal than they are in fact receiving under this measure. This measure is very disappointing, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) knows it. I might say we have nothing against him personally, he is a fellow Albertan and we have always had the highest regard for him. We were pleased that he was appointed Minister of Agriculture but I must say again that the farmers of western Canada expected much more than this when the Conservative government was returned on June 10. Since the election even some of my own supporters, sincere farming people, have come to me and said "It is true that Mr. Diefenbaker is a western man. Do you think we will get a new deal?" They began to talk about him as the golden-haired farm boy. He was from the

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on this bill for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities. Since my remarks are going to be brief I should like to speak particularly in the interests of the fresh fruit and vegetable growers in the province of Ontario.
I have given the bill a great deal of study and have discussed its principal features with a great many farm people. I found that those farm people look upon this bill with confidence that it will provide a sound framework for a much improved farm produce marketing system.
There are two things about the bill which the farmers like in particular. First, it will bring the government closer to the problem of marketing farm produce which is extremely important. Secondly, the advisory board composed of representatives from the agricultural industry as set out in the bill should be able to keep the government well informed on farm problems in general.
The provisions in the bill to provide a constant floor price of 80 per cent average cost over a ten-year period is very sound in my opinion. This will give the farmer a firm foundation price from which to start and will leave him responsible to produce what he can sell in a competitive way at fair prices and in accordance with the supply and demand of Canada's domestic market and the export market.
A higher floor price, as suggested by some hon. members, could bring about surpluses and overproduction which are not desirable. The Canadian farmer wishes to retain his spirit of free enterprise and not become a collective farmer completely under the control of the government. However, there is some other assistance required by specialized farming groups and we must not overlook certain tariff adjustments requested by the fresh fruit and vegetable growers.
In Lincoln county which I represent fresh fruit and vegetables are the main farm produce and form a very important part of the economy of the Niagara peninsula. Fresh fruit and vegetables are not named commodities in the bill but can be included as designated commodities and have a floor price provided, if required, and such a request will probably be made. It is the opinion of the fresh fruit and vegetable growers that since their products are highly perishable their markets must also be protected with seasonal tariffs and anti-dumping duties.
Fresh fruit and vegetable farming in Ontario is a highly specialized type of farming. Three factors must be right: soil conditions, climate and lots of sunshine. We have them in Lincoln county. We have the rich sandy loam, a mild winter climate and lots of summer sunshine. Niagara peninsula is often referred to as the banana belt. Well all has not been well in the banana belt during the past 10 years, the farmers do not have any trouble growing fine fruits and vegetables but they have experienced much
3500	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization trouble in disposing of them. The government has spent many thousands of dollars in experimental stations. Research work done in those experimental stations has been of tremendous value to the fruit and vegetable farmer. New varieties of fruit and vegetables have been discovered and new methods have been found to counteract bugs, grubs and blight, but the marketing of those fine fruits and vegetables has been sadly neglected by the federal government. The Ontario market for fruit and vegetables has been in a constantly depressed condition because of the importation of surplus crops from the United States at distress prices.
The loss of the United Kingdom market for canned fruit and vegetables has been a great blow to the fruit and vegetable growing industry. Every year we have seen more and more of the best fruit farms in the Niagara peninsula subdivided into small holdings and house-building subdivisions. This is not being done because fruit farming is being squeezed out by industry, as we read so often in the newspapers, but because fruit farming in the past 10 years has been too much of a gamble and the farmer has been constantly threatened with being unable to sell his crop. Markets have been too uncertain, and year after year part of the crop has gone to waste on the ground, and that is no lie.
The big problem the Ontario fruit and vegetable farmer has had to contend with is the dumping of surplus crops from the United States on the Canadian markets. The crop season in the United States is from six weeks to 12 weeks ahead of ours. Should there be a surplus crop of any particular fruit or vegetable in the United States, that surplus is dumped on the Canadian market before our crop is ripe and at a cut-rate price. This condition has happened every year for the past 10 years. Some times it is asparagus, strawberries, cherries or peaches. Every year some crop market is ruined by the dumping.
The Niagara fresh fruit and vegetables farmer does not want high tariffs. The farmer does not need high tariffs. He can hold his own under fair marketing conditions. The farmers are asking for a seasonal tariff. This has been on the statute books for many years. It has been asked for continually but has been given only in small measure from six weeks to nine weeks, which is quite ineffective. To be effective it must be for 14 weeks, which is recognized as the crop season for most fruit and vegetables in the province of Ontario. Dumping duties have also been on the statute books for many years. The application of those dumping duties has


also been asked for on many occasions when dumping was particularly bad.
Last June there was a bumper crop of strawberries in the United States. Carloads of them were rolling into Ontario before our crop was ripe, and they were sold on the Canadian market at distressed prices. Dumping duties were again asked for and for the first time in 22 years the Liberal government took steps to put them into effect. The Ontario fresh strawberry crop was protected. However, the irony of it all, as far as the former government was concerned, was that the act did not become effective until two days after the election and I got the credit for it.
It is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker. Do you wish me to continue? I am pretty near the end of my remarks.
